module_title: Introduction to Beekeeping and Bee Biology

lessons.title: The Role of the Hive in a Colony
lessons.body: A beehive is not just a box; it is the colony's home, nursery, food store, and defense fortress. In Africa, where we have both wild and managed colonies, understanding the hive's role helps you build better boxes. The hive provides shelter from rain, sun, and predators. It allows bees to regulate temperature and humidity, essential for brood rearing. Without a proper hive, a colony cannot survive for long. In traditional beekeeping, people use hollow logs, clay pots, or gourds. These work, but they are hard to manage and often destroy the colony during harvest. Modern hives like the Langstroth, Top-Bar, and Warre are designed to mimic natural cavities and allow beekeepers to inspect and harvest without killing bees. The hive also stores honey and pollen. In Africa, honey is a valuable cash crop. A strong colony can produce 20-30 kg of honey per year in a good hive. The hive must be dark, dry, and well-ventilated. Bees need a small entrance that they can defend against robber bees and pests like ants and wax moths. Inside, the hive has frames or bars where bees build comb. The comb is used for brood, honey, and pollen. The hive also serves as a social hub. The queen lays eggs, workers communicate, and drones mate. A well-constructed hive increases colony productivity and makes beekeeping profitable. As you build your hive, remember: you are creating a home for thousands of bees. Every detail matters, from the size of the entrance to the thickness of the walls. A good hive is an investment that pays off in honey and healthy bees.

lessons.title: Basic Anatomy of the Honey Bee
lessons.body: To work with bees, you must know their body parts. The honey bee has three main sections: head, thorax, and abdomen. The head has two large compound eyes, three simple eyes (ocelli), and antennae. The antennae smell and feel. The mouthparts are built for sucking nectar and chewing. The thorax is the middle section, packed with muscles for flight. It has two pairs of wings and three pairs of legs. The legs are specialized: front legs clean antennae, middle legs groom, and hind legs have pollen baskets (corbiculae) for carrying pollen. The abdomen contains the digestive system, heart, and reproductive organs. Workers have a sting at the tip. The sting is a modified ovipositor. When a worker stings, it dies because the sting is barbed and pulls out. The queen's sting is smooth and she can sting multiple times. Drones have no sting. Inside the bee, there is a honey stomach (crop) for carrying nectar. Enzymes in the crop start converting nectar to honey. Bees also have wax glands on the underside of the abdomen. These glands produce beeswax, which they use to build comb. A worker bee can produce about 1/8 of a teaspoon of wax in its lifetime. That's why building comb is energy-intensive. Bees have a tracheal system for breathing, not lungs. Air enters through spiracles on the sides of the body. Understanding anatomy helps you handle bees gently. For example, you avoid crushing them, which releases alarm pheromones. You also know that smoke masks their sense of smell, reducing aggression. Knowing bee anatomy is the first step to becoming a skilled beekeeper.

lessons.title: The Lifecycle of the Honey Bee
lessons.body: The honey bee undergoes complete metamorphosis: egg, larva, pupa, adult. The queen lays eggs in hexagonal cells. Fertilized eggs become females (workers or queens); unfertilized eggs become males (drones). The egg hatches in 3 days into a tiny larva. For the first 3 days, all larvae are fed royal jelly. After that, worker and drone larvae get bee bread (pollen and honey), while queen larvae continue on royal jelly. This diet determines whether a female becomes a queen. The larva grows rapidly, molting five times in about 6 days. Then it spins a cocoon and becomes a pupa. During pupation, the body transforms. The adult emerges by chewing through the wax cap. The development time varies: queen takes 16 days, worker 21 days, drone 24 days. In Africa, these times may be slightly shorter due to warmer temperatures. A queen can lay up to 2,000 eggs per day during peak season. That's more than her own body weight. Workers live 4-6 weeks in summer, but up to 6 months in winter or dearth periods. Drones live about 8 weeks, then are kicked out before winter. The lifecycle is crucial for beekeeping. When you inspect a hive, you look for eggs, larvae, and capped brood to assess queen health. If you see eggs, the queen was there in the last 3 days. If you see only capped brood and no eggs, the queen may be failing. Understanding the timeline helps you plan harvests and colony splits. For example, to raise a new queen, you need to know that she emerges in 16 days. This knowledge is power in beekeeping.

lessons.title: Cast Systems: Queen, Workers, Drones
lessons.body: A honey bee colony has three castes: queen, workers, and drones. Each has a specific role. The queen is the only fertile female. She lays eggs and produces pheromones that control the colony's behavior. A queen can live 2-3 years, but beekeepers often replace her after 1-2 years to maintain productivity. She mates once in her life with 10-20 drones, storing sperm for years. The workers are sterile females. They do all the work: cleaning, nursing, building comb, foraging, guarding, and regulating temperature. Worker jobs change with age. Young workers are nurses; older ones forage. A worker bee visits 50-100 flowers per trip. To make 1 kg of honey, bees must visit about 4 million flowers and fly 90,000 km. That's a lot of work. Workers communicate through dances. The waggle dance tells direction and distance to food. Drones are male bees. They have no sting, no pollen baskets, and no wax glands. Their only job is to mate with a virgin queen. After mating, they die. In a colony, there are a few hundred to a few thousand drones, mostly in the warm season. In Africa, drones are produced year-round in tropical areas. Beekeepers sometimes remove drone comb to control varroa mites, but in Africa, varroa is less of a problem. Understanding castes helps you manage the hive. For example, if you see many drones, it may indicate a failing queen or preparation for swarming. If you see queen cells, the colony may be about to swarm. You can prevent swarming by splitting the colony or removing queen cells. Each caste is essential for the colony's survival. A balanced colony has one queen, thousands of workers, and a few hundred drones.

lessons.title: Understanding Bee Space and Propolis
lessons.body: Bee space is the gap that bees leave open between combs. It is about 6-9 mm (1/4 to 3/8 inch). If the gap is smaller, bees fill it with propolis. If larger, they build burr comb. This discovery by Lorenzo Langstroth revolutionized beekeeping. In Africa, bee space is critical for building hives that are easy to work with. When you build a Langstroth hive, you must maintain 6-9 mm between frames. If you don't, bees will glue everything together with propolis, making inspection difficult. Propolis is a resinous mixture that bees collect from tree buds, sap, and other plant sources. They use it to seal cracks, strengthen comb, and sanitize the hive. Propolis has antimicrobial properties. In Africa, propolis is harvested for medicinal use and sold in markets. It can fetch good prices. But too much propolis is a nuisance for beekeepers. To minimize propolis, keep your hive tools clean and avoid leaving gaps. Also, choose bee strains that use less propolis. In Top-Bar hives, bee space is maintained by the width of the bars. The bars are usually 32-35 mm wide, which gives the correct spacing. In Warre hives, the boxes are designed with proper bee space. When building your hive, measure carefully. A small mistake can lead to a glued-up hive. Also, bees use propolis to narrow the entrance. You can scrape it off during inspections. But leave some, as it helps with defense. Understanding bee space and propolis is key to a manageable hive. It saves you time and reduces stress on the bees.

lessons.title: Overview of Hive Types: Langstroth, Top-Bar, Warre
lessons.body: There are three main modern hive types used in Africa: Langstroth, Top-Bar, and Warre. Each has advantages and disadvantages. The Langstroth hive is the most common. It has stacked boxes with movable frames. The frames allow you to inspect and harvest honey without destroying comb. A standard Langstroth hive has 10 frames per box. The boxes are called supers. You can add supers as the colony grows. Langstroth hives produce the most honey, up to 30-40 kg per year in good conditions. They are easy to transport and manage. However, they require precise construction and are more expensive. The Top-Bar hive is simpler. It has a single box with bars across the top. Bees build comb hanging from the bars. You can inspect each bar individually. Top-Bar hives are cheaper to build and easier for beginners. They are good for areas where wood is scarce. But they produce less honey, about 15-20 kg per year, and the comb is fragile. You cannot extract honey with a centrifuge; you must crush and strain. The Warre hive is like a Top-Bar but with boxes stacked vertically. It is designed to mimic a tree cavity. Warre hives are less intrusive; you add boxes to the bottom. They produce about 20-25 kg per year. They are good for natural beekeeping. In Africa, the choice depends on your goals, budget, and local conditions. Langstroth is best for commercial honey production. Top-Bar is good for small-scale and beginners. Warre is for those who want a more natural approach. Many African beekeepers use a mix. For example, you can start with a Top-Bar and later switch to Langstroth. Whatever you choose, ensure the hive has proper bee space, ventilation, and a secure entrance. Your hive is your farm; choose wisely.

quiz.q: What is the primary role of the hive in a bee colony?
options: B) To provide shelter, nursery, and food storage
D) To keep out all insects
quiz.explanation: The hive serves as shelter, nursery, and food storage, and provides defense.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT a traditional hive material in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Plastic boxes are modern, not traditional.

quiz.q: How much honey can a strong colony produce per year in a good hive?
quiz.explanation: A strong colony can produce 20-30 kg of honey per year.

quiz.q: What is the function of the antennae on a honey bee?
quiz.explanation: Antennae are sensory organs for smell and touch.

quiz.q: Where are pollen baskets located on a worker bee?
quiz.explanation: Pollen baskets (corbiculae) are on the hind legs.

quiz.q: What happens to a worker bee after it stings?
options: C) It loses its sting but lives
quiz.explanation: The barbed sting pulls out, causing the worker to die.

quiz.q: How many eggs can a queen lay per day during peak season?
quiz.explanation: A queen can lay up to 2,000 eggs per day.

quiz.q: What determines whether a female larva becomes a queen?
quiz.explanation: Queen larvae are fed royal jelly throughout development.

quiz.q: How long does it take for a worker bee to develop from egg to adult?
quiz.explanation: Worker bees take 21 days to develop.

quiz.q: What is the role of drones in a colony?
quiz.explanation: Drones' only role is to mate with a virgin queen.

quiz.q: How many times does a queen mate in her life?
quiz.explanation: A queen mates once, storing sperm for life.

quiz.q: What is bee space?
options: B) The gap bees leave open between combs
C) The size of the entrance
quiz.explanation: Bee space is the 6-9 mm gap bees leave between combs.

quiz.q: What do bees use propolis for?
quiz.explanation: Propolis is used to seal cracks and has antimicrobial properties.

quiz.q: Which hive type uses movable frames?
quiz.explanation: Langstroth hives have movable frames.

quiz.q: What is a disadvantage of Top-Bar hives?
quiz.explanation: Top-Bar comb is fragile and cannot be centrifuged.

quiz.q: How many frames are typically in a Langstroth hive box?
quiz.explanation: A standard Langstroth box holds 10 frames.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of a Warre hive?
quiz.explanation: Warre hives mimic tree cavities and are less intrusive.

quiz.q: What does the waggle dance communicate?
options: B) Direction and distance to food
quiz.explanation: The waggle dance tells other bees where food is.

quiz.q: How many flowers must bees visit to make 1 kg of honey?
quiz.explanation: Bees visit about 4 million flowers to make 1 kg of honey.

quiz.q: What is royal jelly?
options: B) A secretion from nurse bees
quiz.explanation: Royal jelly is a nutritious secretion fed to larvae and queens.

quiz.q: Which caste has no sting?
quiz.explanation: Drones are male and have no sting.

quiz.q: What is the typical lifespan of a worker bee in summer?
quiz.explanation: Summer workers live 4-6 weeks due to hard work.

quiz.q: What does a beekeeper look for to assess queen health?
options: B) Presence of eggs and larvae
quiz.explanation: Eggs and larvae indicate a laying queen.

quiz.q: What is the ideal bee space in millimeters?
quiz.explanation: Bee space is 6-9 mm.

quiz.q: What happens if bee space is too small?
options: B) Bees fill it with propolis
quiz.explanation: Small gaps are filled with propolis.

quiz.q: Which hive type is best for commercial honey production?
quiz.explanation: Langstroth hives produce the most honey.

quiz.q: What is the function of the honey stomach?
quiz.explanation: The honey stomach (crop) carries nectar back to the hive.

quiz.q: How long does a queen take to develop from egg to adult?
quiz.explanation: Queens develop in 16 days.

quiz.q: What is propolis made from?
quiz.explanation: Propolis is made from tree resins and other plant sources.

quiz.q: Which hive type is stacked vertically and added to the bottom?
quiz.explanation: Warre hives are added to the bottom.
